original_excerpt:
Baker v. Carr, 369 U.S. 186, 197–198, 237 (1962):
The Supreme Court limited its decision to procedural and threshold jurisdictional questions, ruling that voter challenges to legislative apportionment under the Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause are justiciable in federal court and do not present a non-justiciable political question. Justice Brennan made clear that the Court was not reaching the merits or defining the substantive constitutional standards of equality required for legislative apportionment.
Reynolds v. Sims, 377 U.S. 533, 556, 568 (1964):
The Supreme Court recognized that Baker v. Carr had resolved only the threshold issue of justiciability without determining the substantive rules governing apportionment schemes. Reynolds then established the substantive constitutional rule requiring that seats across both chambers of a bicameral state legislature be apportioned on a population basis to afford voters substantially equal representation.
fidelity: Threshold/justiciability versus population-based substantive standard accurately summarized; Baker does not decide ultimate apportionment merits.
scope_note: Reynolds requires substantial population equality, not mathematical exactness. Gray merely listed and not independently established by Column N.
